metadata.paperYaml:
# The one source of publication metadata for White Repopulation.
# CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json, codemeta.json and metadata/scholarly-article.jsonld
# are generated from this file by @red-cup-engineering/research-release-metadata-service
# (`make metadata`); `make metadata-check` fails if any of them drifts from it.
# The schema is that service's schemas/paper.schema.json.
id: white-repopulation
title: "White Repopulation: Reproduction without Preservation"
subtitle: "The future white, captive births, and the transatlantic reproduction of settler rule"
version: "0.2.0"
year: 2026
date-released: "2026-10-24"
status: released
publication-type: preprint
peer-reviewed: false
access-right: open
language: en-US
abstract: >-
  Settler institutions in the United States have described their future as the
  increase of a white population. That description joins four histories that
  move independently: the births and survival of people counted as white; the
  changing rules for who counts; eligibility to found a preferred future
  population; and the reproduction of property, jurisdiction and labor
  relations. This study separates them and asks which one institutions
  preserved when they conflicted. Four documentary and quantitative strands
  answer in turn. Franklin's population arithmetic, race-suicide pronatalism
  and Virginia's racial-integrity law show a purity ideal that bent when its
  rigid application threatened elite genealogies. A reconstruction of births,
  1790–1859, finds that roughly one U.S. birth in six (17.20% in 1800–1849)
  was a birth into hereditary slavery, a reproduction of property that
  conferred no membership. Antebellum property law divided a child's status,
  title and anticipated issue across time. Transatlantic sending, receiving
  and policy-borrowing cases show settler growth drawing on selected,
  indebted and assisted migrants through case-specific institutions rather
  than one coordinated design. Across the strands, institutions
  preserved the authority to classify and to appropriate reproduction more
  reliably than the reproductive opportunities of every person classified
  white. The stronger proposition, that a deferred ideal can exhaust the
  population it claims to protect, remains a conditional hypothesis; the paper
  states the cohort and institutional evidence that would test it.
keywords:
  - settler colonialism
  - social reproduction
  - historical sociology
  - historical demography
  - racial formation
  - slavery
  - eugenics
  - reproductive futurity
  - migration

  - term: History and archaeology

    Quoted historical documents, archival transcriptions and third-party works

    family: Sennhauser

    role: accountable-author
    ai: false

    affiliation: Disclosed AI research collaborator
    role: ai-research-collaborator
    ai: true

contributors:
  - name: Claude (Anthropic)
    ai: true
    role: integration, reproducible-build and release engineering
    zenodo-type: Other
    disclosure: >-
      Claude is an AI system. It assembled the integrated edition, wrote the
      introduction and conclusion from the parts' findings, and built the

acknowledgements:
  - name: Anonymous contributor
    role: research direction
ai-disclosure:
  statement: >-
    AI systems performed most source retrieval, drafting, quantitative
    reconstruction and release engineering under direction of the accountable
    author. Every quantitative claim is recomputed from the archived records by
    the claim specification in claims/; every source carries a reading grade recording how
    much of it was actually read. Readers should weigh claims by those grades.
care:
  collective-benefit: >-
    The study concerns people whose reproduction was appropriated by settler
    institutions, and Indigenous nations whose recognition those institutions
    conditioned. Findings are released openly so descendant communities and
    their scholars can use, contest and correct them without cost.
  authority-to-control: >-
    No Indigenous data are collected. Where the paper discusses Indigenous
    political continuity (for example Pamunkey opposition to Virginia's 1930
    law), it relies on published scholarship and public records, and treats
    colonial administrative recognition as distinct from Indigenous
    self-determination. Requests from a named nation concerning those passages
    are handled under docs/data-governance.md.
  responsibility: >-
    Source records state what each document can and cannot show, including
    the bias of court and enslaver records that seldom preserve the voices of
    enslaved mothers and children.
  ethics: >-
    Persons named in historical records are not reduced to counts; the paper
    does not reproduce identifying detail beyond what its published sources
    already make public.
related-identifiers:
  - relation: isSupplementedBy
    identifier: https://github.com/lenticule-science/sociology-science-services-section
    scheme: url
message: >-
  Please cite the versioned release of this preprint. It is not peer
  reviewed, and no DOI is assigned until an archived release mints one.
limitations:
  - "historical births: retrospective modeled estimates; 1790s denominator assumed; no measured prevalence of coerced conception"
  - "historical migration: all-population national rates; not white-specific or local lineage survival"
  - "legal cases: purposive judicial comparison; title and status variation, not population frequency"
  - "self-consuming futurity: a historical hypothesis, not a demonstrated causal demographic law"
